Can anyone help me solve this probability puzzle? I've included pics of the puzzle, a hint, my work, and the app on the app store if anyone wants to try it.

Everything is OK up to where you find the probability of a particular family having all boys or all girls is 0.51^8 + 0.49^8, however multiplying that by 50 families takes you off track. The trick is to then note that the probability that both genders are present in any particular family is 1-(.49^8+.51^8), and that each of 50 families having both genders is [1-(.49^8+.51^8)]^50. Then 1-[1-(.49^8+.51^8)]^50 is the probability you want.

Note: multiplying by 50 isn't completely meaningless. It does give the expected number of single-gender families, but that is higher than the probability of finding any single-gender families because of the possibility that a sample of 50 might have several single gender families. (If you flip a coin 3 times, you expect to get 1.5 heads, but the probability of getting any heads at all is only 7/8.)

Yeah, there's basically two laws for discrete probability (every other formula you're like to meet is just a special case of some combination of these two).

The addition rule says that if two events are mutually exclusive, then P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

The multiplication rule says that if two events are independent, then P(A and B) = P(A) * P(B).

This problem uses a special case of the addition rule to justify P(A) = P(A or notA) - P(notA) = 1 - P(notA)

It also uses the multiplication rule. Since the makeup of each family is independent of every other family, the probability of all of them having some particular makeup is the product of each family individually having that makeup.

When a probability raised to an exponent appears in a solution, it usually (as it did in this case) means that there were a bunch of independent events which all had the same probability of happening, and you wanted to evaluate the probability that all of them happen simultaneously.

"White Rabbit" was written and performed by Grace Slick while she was still with The Great Society. When that band broke up in 1966, Slick was invited to join Jefferson Airplane to replace their departed female singer, Signe Toly Anderson, who left the band with the birth of her child. The first album Slick recorded with Jefferson Airplane was Surrealistic Pillow, and Slick provided two songs from her previous group: her own "White Rabbit" and "Somebody to Love", written by her brother-in-law Darby Slick and recorded under the title "Someone to Love" by The Great Society. The Great Society's version of "White Rabbit" was much longer than the more aggressive version of Jefferson Airplane. The song was ranked number 478 on Rolling Stone's list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time, Number 87 on Rate Your Music's Top Singles of All Time, and appears on The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame's 500 Songs that Shaped Rock and Roll.

"White Rabbit" is one of Grace Slick's earliest songs, written during either late 1965 or early 1966. It uses imagery found in the fantasy works of Lewis Carroll—1865's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland and its 1871 sequel Through the Looking-Glass—such as changing size after taking pills or drinking an unknown liquid.

Slick had stated the composition was intended to be a slap to parents who read their children such novels and then wondered why their children later used drugs. Characters Slick referenced include Alice, the White Rabbit, the hookah-smoking caterpillar, the White Knight, the Red Queen, and the Dormouse. Slick reportedly wrote the song after an acid trip. For Slick, "White Rabbit" "is about following your curiosity. The White Rabbit is your curiosity". For her and others in the 1960s, drugs were a part of mind expansion and social experimentation. With its enigmatic lyrics, "White Rabbit" became one of the first songs to sneak drug references past censors on the radio. Even Marty Balin, Slick's eventual rival in Jefferson Airplane, regarded the song as a "masterpiece". In interviews, Slick has related that Alice in Wonderland was often read to her as a child and remained a vivid memory well into her adulthood. Slick mentioned that in addition to Alice in Wonderland, her other inspiration for the song was "the bolero used by Miles Davis and Gil Evans on their 1960 album Sketches of Spain." The song is essentially one long crescendo similar to that of Ravel's famous "Boléro". The music combined with the song's lyrics strongly suggests the sensory distortions experienced with hallucinogens, and the song was later used in pop culture to imply or accompany just such a state.
